questions.question: What is event-driven architecture?

options.text: Architecture based on scheduled batch jobs
Architecture where components communicate by producing and consuming events
Architecture using only synchronous REST APIs
Architecture without any inter-service communication

questions.explanation: Event-driven architecture: components communicate through events (facts about what happened). Producers emit events without knowing consumers. LinkedIn processes 7 trillion events daily through Kafka. This enables loose coupling, scalability, and real-time responsiveness. It's the backbone of modern data pipelines at Netflix, Uber, and Airbnb.

questions.question: What is an 'event' in event-driven architecture?

options.text: A request for another service to perform an action
An immutable record of something that happened
A database query result
A scheduled task execution

questions.explanation: An event is a fact—an immutable record of something that occurred: 'OrderPlaced', 'PaymentReceived', 'UserRegistered'. Events describe what happened (past tense), not what should happen. They're immutable because you can't change history. This distinction from commands (requests for action) is fundamental to event-driven design.

questions.question: Which are benefits of event-driven architecture? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Loose coupling between components
Better scalability through async processing
Simpler debugging than synchronous systems
Real-time responsiveness

questions.explanation: EDA benefits: loose coupling (producers don't know consumers—add new consumers without changing producers), scalability (async processing, independent scaling of producers and consumers), real-time (react to events immediately). Debugging is HARDER—tracing event flows across services requires distributed tracing tools like Jaeger. The complexity is the tradeoff for flexibility.

questions.question: What is the difference between events and commands?

options.text: No functional difference, just naming conventions
Events describe what happened; commands request an action
Commands are faster to process than events
Events are synchronous; commands are asynchronous

questions.explanation: Events: past tense, describe facts ('OrderPlaced', 'UserCreated'). Commands: imperative, request action ('PlaceOrder', 'CreateUser'). Events are broadcast to interested parties; commands are sent to specific handlers. A command might fail; an event already happened. This semantic difference affects system design: events enable loose coupling, commands imply direct relationships.

questions.question: What is an event broker?

options.text: A person who manages event planning
Infrastructure that receives, stores, and delivers events between producers and consumers
A relational database for event storage
A load balancer for event traffic

questions.explanation: Event broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS EventBridge, Google Pub/Sub) is the messaging infrastructure. It receives events from producers, stores them (Kafka retains for days/weeks), and delivers to consumers. The broker decouples producers from consumers—they never communicate directly. Kafka handles trillions of messages daily at LinkedIn; AWS EventBridge routes events across AWS services.

questions.question: What challenge does event ordering present?

options.text: Events are always delivered in perfect order
Events may arrive out of order; consumers must handle this
Ordering is irrelevant in event-driven systems
Events cannot be ordered under any circumstances

questions.explanation: In distributed systems, events may arrive out of order due to network delays, partitioning, or parallel processing. If 'OrderShipped' arrives before 'OrderPlaced', consumers must handle this gracefully. Solutions: use timestamps/sequence numbers, partition by entity ID (all events for order-123 go to same partition), or design for order-independence. Kafka guarantees order within a partition, not across partitions.

questions.question: True or False: Event-driven architecture guarantees exactly-once event processing.

options.text: True - modern event brokers guarantee exactly-once delivery
False - most systems provide at-least-once; consumers must be idempotent

questions.explanation: Most event systems provide at-least-once delivery (events may be duplicated due to retries, network issues, or consumer failures). Exactly-once is extremely difficult in distributed systems—Kafka added 'exactly-once semantics' but it requires specific configurations and has limitations. Consumers must be idempotent—handle duplicate events safely. Use idempotency keys, deduplication tables, or design operations to be naturally idempotent.

questions.question: What is 'event sourcing'?

options.text: Finding the origin of events for debugging
Storing all state changes as a sequence of events, deriving current state from event history
Deleting old events to save storage
Compressing events for efficient transmission

questions.explanation: Event sourcing: instead of storing current state, store all events that led to current state. Current state is derived by replaying events. A bank account's balance is the sum of all deposits and withdrawals. This provides complete audit trail, enables temporal queries ('what was the state last Tuesday?'), and supports rebuilding state. LMAX Exchange uses event sourcing for their trading platform.

questions.question: Which scenarios are well-suited for event-driven architecture? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Real-time notifications and alerts
Audit logging and compliance tracking
Simple CRUD applications with few users
Decoupled microservices communication

questions.explanation: EDA suits: real-time notifications (react to events immediately—Slack notifications), audit logging (events are natural audit trail—financial compliance), microservices (loose coupling via events—Uber's trip events). Simple CRUD may not need EDA complexity—synchronous REST calls are simpler and sufficient. Don't add distributed systems complexity without clear benefits.

questions.question: What is 'eventual consistency' in event-driven systems?

options.text: Data is always immediately consistent across all services
Data will become consistent across services after events are processed, but may be temporarily inconsistent
Data is never consistent between services
Consistency is not a concern in event-driven systems

questions.explanation: Eventual consistency: after an event, different services may temporarily have different views of data. Eventually, all services process the event and converge to consistent state. When you post on Twitter, your followers might see it at slightly different times. This is the tradeoff for availability and scalability—strong consistency requires coordination that limits throughput. Design UIs to handle temporary inconsistency gracefully.

questions.question: How should event consumers handle failures?

options.text: Crash and lose the event permanently
Retry with backoff; use dead letter queues for persistent failures
Ignore failures and continue processing
Stop processing all events until manual intervention

questions.explanation: Consumers should: retry failed processing with exponential backoff (handle transient failures), move persistently failing events to dead letter queue (DLQ) for investigation, and be idempotent (safe to retry). AWS SQS, Kafka, and RabbitMQ all support DLQs. Never lose events silently—they represent business facts. Monitor DLQ depth as a health metric.

questions.question: What is the 'event notification' pattern?

options.text: Sending push notifications to mobile devices
Events contain minimal data; consumers fetch details from source if needed
Events contain complete data for all possible consumers
Events are not persisted, only transmitted

questions.explanation: Event notification: events contain minimal info (entity ID, event type, timestamp). Consumers call back to the source service for full data if needed. This reduces event size and avoids including data consumers don't need. Tradeoff: adds coupling (consumers depend on source availability) and latency (extra call). Alternative: 'event-carried state transfer' includes full data in events. Choose based on your consistency and coupling requirements.
